identification.summary: Ghost Blizzard is the Microsoft name for a Russia-origin actor that Microsoft maps to BROMINE, Berserk Bear, TG-4192, Koala Team, Blue Kraken, Crouching Yeti and Dragonfly [S1]. MITRE ATT&CK tracks it as Dragonfly (G0035): a cyber espionage group attributed to Russia's FSB Center 16 that has targeted defense and aviation companies, government entities, ICS-related companies and critical-infrastructure sectors worldwide through supply-chain, spearphishing and drive-by compromise [S2]. The group is best known for long-running access operations against Western energy companies, including trojanized ICS vendor software (2013-2014) [S3][S4] and the 'Dragonfly 2.0' campaign against energy firms in Europe and North America [S5][S6].
identification.firstObserved: MITRE: active since at least 2010 [S2]. Symantec (as reported in 2017 coverage): active since at least 2011 [S5]. The US indictment covers activity from about 2012 to 2017-2018 [S9].
identification.notes: Microsoft name: Ghost Blizzard (former Microsoft name BROMINE) [S1]. US and UK government statements describe the team as a unit within FSB Center 16, also known as Military Unit 71330 [S9][S10][S13]. Cisco Talos tracks 'Static Tundra', which it assesses with high confidence is a subset of Berserk Bear active since at least 2015; that is a sub-cluster, not a full alias [S11]. The imported summary in this record came from Dragos's ALLANITE profile; Dragos tracks ALLANITE (and DYMALLOY) as its own ICS-focused clusters, so ALLANITE details should not be merged into Ghost Blizzard without Dragos's own mapping (see gaps).

attribution.sponsor: Russian Federation, Federal Security Service (FSB) Center 16 (Military Unit 71330), per US indictment and UK government attribution [S9][S10][S13].
attribution.confidence: The UK NCSC assessed it 'almost certain' that FSB Centre 16 carried out a malign cyber programme against critical IT systems and national infrastructure in Europe, the Americas and Asia [S10]. A US grand jury in the District of Kansas indicted three FSB Center 16 officers (Pavel Akulov, Mikhail Gavrilov, Marat Tyukov) on 2021-08-26; the indictment was unsealed on 2022-03-24 [S9][S13]. In August 2025 the FBI attributed exploitation of Cisco devices to FSB Center 16 actors, and Cisco Talos assessed with high confidence that the related Static Tundra cluster is a subset of Berserk Bear [S11]. Microsoft's public mapping lists the actor as Russia-origin; no Microsoft confidence statement was found [S1].
attribution.basis: US criminal indictment and State Department Rewards for Justice offer [S9][S12][S13]; UK FCDO/NCSC attribution [S10]; joint DHS/FBI and CISA/FBI advisories [S6][S8]; German BSI/BfV/BND memo [S7]; vendor reporting from Symantec, F-Secure/Netresec and Cisco Talos [S3][S4][S5][S11].

objectives: Long-term espionage and pre-positioned access to critical infrastructure, especially energy. Symantec assessed that Dragonfly 2.0 aimed both to learn how energy facilities operate and to gain access to operational systems, and that this access could enable disruption [S5]. The 2014 trojanized-software campaign was assessed by Symantec as giving the group a beachhead that could enable sabotage, though it focused on espionage at the time [S3]. German agencies warned in 2020 that the group sought to anchor itself permanently in IT networks and possibly reach OT networks [S7]. Public reporting has found no disruptive attack by this actor [S7][S8].

sectors: Energy: electricity grid operators, generation firms, petroleum pipeline operators [S3]
Nuclear (including Wolf Creek Nuclear Operating Corporation) [S6][S10][S12]
ICS / industrial equipment vendors and supply-chain suppliers [S3][S4][S6]
US state, local, territorial and tribal (SLTT) government; US federal agencies [S8][S9]
Telecommunications, higher education and manufacturing (Static Tundra sub-cluster) [S11]
regions: Europe, including Spain, France, Italy, Germany, Poland, Turkey and Switzerland [S3][S5][S7]
Roughly 135 countries per the US indictment [S9]
North America, Asia, Africa and Europe (Static Tundra) [S11]
targeting.notes: The US indictment alleges the Dragonfly 2.0 phase targeted more than 3,300 users at over 500 US and international companies and entities, including US government agencies [S9]. DHS/FBI described staging through smaller, less secure supply-chain organizations before reaching intended energy targets [S6].

capabilities.summary: Supply-chain compromise of ICS vendor websites to trojanize legitimate software installers with the Havex/Oldrea RAT (for example a European PLC maker's driver package available for at least six weeks in June-July 2013) [S3][S4]; custom malware Backdoor.Oldrea and Trojan.Karagany [S3]; spearphishing (including template-based credential harvesting with the Phishery toolkit) and watering-hole websites [S5][S6]; use of common administration tools rather than zero-days after initial access [S5]; network reconnaissance and collection of ICS information inside energy networks [S6]; exploitation of public-facing vulnerabilities including Citrix CVE-2019-19781, Fortinet CVE-2018-13379, Exchange CVE-2020-0688, Exim CVE-2019-10149 and Netlogon CVE-2020-1472 [S8]; and exploitation of Cisco Smart Install CVE-2018-0171 to collect configuration files from thousands of network devices and modify configurations for access [S11].

campaigns.name: Trojanized ICS vendor software (Dragonfly / Havex)
campaigns.summary: Dragonfly compromised ICS equipment vendors and placed the Havex/Oldrea RAT in legitimate software downloads, including a PLC driver package (June-July 2013) and a wind-turbine/biogas management vendor's software (April 2014).

campaigns.name: Public exposure of Dragonfly / Energetic Bear
campaigns.summary: Symantec and F-Secure publicly report the campaign against energy firms in the US and Europe; F-Secure counts 88 Havex variants and 146 C2 servers.

campaigns.name: Dragonfly 2.0 begins
campaigns.summary: Symantec reports renewed activity from late 2015 against energy companies in Europe and North America, using phishing, watering holes and trojanized software.

campaigns.name: Wolf Creek nuclear plant targeting
campaigns.summary: Center 16 targets networks associated with the Wolf Creek nuclear plant in Kansas; the UK says there was no negative impact.

campaigns.name: DHS/FBI alert TA18-074A
campaigns.summary: US government attributes a multi-stage campaign, active since at least March 2016, against energy, nuclear, water, aviation and critical manufacturing to Russian government actors.

campaigns.name: German energy and water supply-chain compromises
campaigns.summary: BSI, BfV and BND warn operators that Berserk Bear had long-standing compromises in German energy, water and power companies via supply chains.

campaigns.name: SLTT and aviation network intrusions (AA20-296A)
campaigns.summary: CISA/FBI report targeting of dozens of US SLTT and aviation networks since at least September 2020, with data exfiltrated from at least two servers by 1 October 2020.

campaigns.name: US indictment unsealed; UK attribution
campaigns.summary: DOJ unseals the Kansas indictment of three FSB Center 16 officers for the Dragonfly campaigns; the UK attributes the programme to FSB Centre 16.

campaigns.name: Cisco Smart Install exploitation (Static Tundra)
campaigns.summary: FBI warns that FSB Center 16 actors exploited CVE-2018-0171 to harvest configurations from thousands of US critical-infrastructure network devices; Cisco Talos tracks the activity as Static Tundra, a Berserk Bear subset.

campaigns.name: Rewards for Justice offer
campaigns.summary: US State Department offers up to $10 million for information on the three indicted FSB officers.

diamond.adversary: FSB Center 16 (Military Unit 71330); three officers indicted in the US (Akulov, Gavrilov, Tyukov) [S9][S10][S13].
diamond.capability: Havex/Oldrea and Karagany malware; trojanized ICS software; spearphishing and watering holes; public-facing VPN, Citrix, Exchange and Cisco Smart Install exploits [S3][S5][S8][S11].
diamond.infrastructure: Compromised ICS vendor download sites [S3][S4]; compromised small supply-chain organizations used as staging targets [S6]; watering-hole websites [S5][S6]; Havex C2 servers (146 counted by F-Secure) [S3].
diamond.victim: Energy, nuclear, water and aviation organizations, ICS vendors, US SLTT and federal government, and network devices at telecom, education and manufacturing organizations [S3][S6][S8][S11].
diamond.socioPolitical: Russian state interest in mapping and holding access to Western critical infrastructure, especially energy [S5][S7][S10].
diamond.technology: Windows enterprise networks bridging to ICS environments; trusted vendor update channels; internet-facing VPN/remote-access appliances and legacy Cisco IOS devices with Smart Install enabled [S3][S6][S8][S11].

gaps: Microsoft has published little actor-specific reporting under the Ghost Blizzard name; only Microsoft's public name mapping was found [S1]. learn.microsoft.com could not be fetched.

Primary government documents could not be opened (cisa.gov, justice.gov and ic3.gov blocked): TA18-074A, AA20-296A, the Akulov indictment and the FBI August 2025 PSA are cited through press or search-result coverage [S6][S8][S11][S13].
Symantec's 2014 and 2017 Dragonfly reports, Secureworks IRON LIBERTY, Dragos ALLANITE/DYMALLOY and the MITRE G0035 page could not be fetched; facts rely on search excerpts and press coverage.

Cluster boundaries: Dragos tracks ALLANITE and DYMALLOY separately; the imported ALLANITE summary may not describe Ghost Blizzard as Microsoft scopes it. Cisco Talos's Static Tundra is described as a subset of Berserk Bear, not the whole group [S11]. MITRE also keeps a separate Dragonfly 2.0 entry (G0074) [S2].

The UK FSB factsheet (updated December 2023) reportedly lists Turla/Snake/Venomous Bear names alongside Energetic Bear under the FSB structure; whether this reflects one unit or a grouping by parent organisation was not verified [S10].
Sources disagree on campaign end dates (indictment summaries give 2012-2017 or 2012-2018) [S9].
Activity after Russia's 2022 invasion of Ukraine, aside from the 2025 Cisco device exploitation, is not documented in the sources gathered.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1 (OE): Key terrain is the IT/OT boundary at energy, nuclear, water and aviation facilities, the vendor software-update channels that feed them, and internet-facing VPN, Citrix, Exchange and legacy Cisco network devices [S3][S6][S8][S11]. Installations relying on commercial utilities inherit this exposure. STEP 2 (effects): The actor has used trusted vendor downloads and smaller suppliers to reach hardened targets, so a defended perimeter does not bound the threat [S3][S6]. Unpatched years-old CVEs remain viable entry points [S11]. STEP 3 (adversary template): Supply-chain or phishing/watering-hole access, then credential harvest, admin-tool lateral movement, ICS reconnaissance and screenshots, with persistence and no observed disruption [S5][S6][S8]. STEP 4: MLCOA is continued quiet access and collection of ICS and network-device configuration data from critical infrastructure [S7][S11]. MDCOA is use of that pre-positioned access to disrupt energy or other utility operations during a crisis, which Symantec and German agencies flagged as possible but which has not been observed [S5][S7]. Candidate indicators: unexpected Smart Install (TCP 4786) traffic or configuration exfiltration from Cisco devices [S11]; SMB/credential-harvesting template injections in phishing documents [S5]; new local accounts and remote access on engineering hosts; anomalous downloads from ICS vendor sites [S3][S6].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. Situational awareness: Track the actor's targeting of commercial energy, water and aviation providers and of SLTT networks that support installations, alongside DODIN assets, since the reported victims sit largely outside DoD networks [S6][S8]. Authorities: Most likely victims are private-sector or civil-government owners, so response relies on coordination with CISA, FBI and DOE rather than DoD action on those networks [S6][S8][S9]. Mission assurance: Prioritise mission-relevant dependencies on commercial power and on legacy network devices; patch or disable Cisco Smart Install and harden internet-facing remote-access appliances named in advisories [S8][S11]. Coordination: Share indicators across energy-sector ISACs and allied partners, since the UK, Germany and the US have each reported the same actor [S7][S9][S10].
